Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. The idea is simple yet effective – during training, we will randomly “drop” with some probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o000⟧ a subset of neurons during each forward / backward pass (or equivalently, we will keep alive each neuron with a probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o001⟧ ). Then, during testing, we will use the full network to compute our predictions. The result is that the network typically learns more meaningful information from the data, is less likely to overfit, and usually obtains higher performance overall on the task at hand. One intuitive reason why this technique should be so effective is that what dropout is doing is essentially doing is training exponentially many smaller networks at once and averaging over their predictions.

Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. The idea is simple yet effective – during training, we will randomly “drop” with some probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o000⟧ a subset of neurons during each forward / backward pass (or equivalently, we will keep alive each neuron with a probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o001⟧ ). The result is that the network typically learns more meaningful information from the data, is less likely to overfit, and usually obtains higher performance overall on the task at hand. One intuitive reason why this technique should be so effective is that what dropout is doing is essentially doing is training exponentially many smaller networks at once and averaging over their predictions.

Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. The idea is simple yet effective – during training, we will randomly “drop” with some probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o000⟧ a subset of neurons during each forward / backward pass (or equivalently, we will keep alive each neuron with a probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o001⟧ ). Then, during testing, we will use the full network to compute our predictions. The result is that the network typically learns more meaningful information from the data, is less likely to overfit, and usually obtains higher performance overall on the task at hand. One intuitive reason why this technique should be so effective is that what dropout is doing is essentially doing is training exponentially many smaller networks at once and averaging over their predictions.

After a rigorous mathematical discussion of neural networks, we will discuss some practical tips and tricks in training neural networks involving: neuron units (non-linearities), gradient checks, Xavier parameter initialization, learning rates, Adagrad, etc. Lastly, we will motivate the use of recurrent neural networks as a language model.

Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. The idea is simple yet effective – during training, we will randomly “drop” with some probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o000⟧ a subset of neurons during each forward / backward pass (or equivalently, we will keep alive each neuron with a probability ⟦P:a-native-1c29d0561e00-g0122-o001⟧ ). Then, during testing, we will use the full network to compute our predictions. The result is that the network typically learns more meaningful information from the data, is less likely to overfit, and usually obtains higher performance overall on the task at hand. One intuitive reason why this technique should be so effective is that what dropout is doing is essentially doing is training exponentially many smaller networks at once and averaging over their predictions.

Now, a natural question you might ask is, if this method is so precise, why do we not use it to compute all of our network gradients instead of applying back-propagation? The simple answer, as hinted earlier, is inefficiency – recall that every time we want to compute the gradient with respect to an element, we need to make two forward passes through the network, which will be computationally expensive. Furthermore, many large-scale neural networks can contain millions of parameters, and computing two passes per parameter is clearly not optimal. And, since in optimization techniques such as SGD, we must compute the gradients once per iteration for several thousands of iterations, it is obvious that this method quickly grows intractable. This inefficiency is why we only use gradient check to verify the correctness of our analytic gradients, which are much quicker to compute. Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. Dropout is a powerful technique for regularization, first introduced by Srivastava et al. in Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.
